generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology gives you a ready language for the differences behind team conflict. The OCEAN model, which you may meet in a personality module, names five factors: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Used with care, and without boxing people in, this framework helps you see why a teammate pushes a bold design or urges caution, so you can respond to the person rather than only to the position. Reflecting on that with a judgement, rather than a description, is itself a psychological skill employers value.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students are in a team where the designer and the analyst are arguing hard over how to present the results, two days before the poster session.

Tom finds the row stressful and stays quiet, hoping it will pass. Asked later to reflect, he writes that 'there was a disagreement but we sorted it in the end'. The conflict was neither helped nor understood, and the reflection only describes what happened. Nothing was learned that could be carried into the next team.

Amara sees that the designer is an innovator and the analyst a cautious realist, both right in part. She acknowledges each view, then proposes keeping the clear figures the analyst wants while adding one bold visual the designer suggested. Reflecting afterwards, she writes that stepping in early, and naming the strengths on both sides, was what held the team together, and would do so again. That is a judgement, and it names a transferable skill.

Both saw the same argument. Only Amara resolved it and learned something sayable from it.
generatedProse.summary: Handling conflict in psychology starts with recognising difference, and your discipline gives you a language for it. Reflecting well means judging your performance, not just describing events, and naming what you have gained. You can now do both, and articulate the transferable-skills value of presenting and group work. With authority, collaboration and reflection in place, you are ready to present and work in teams like a psychology graduate.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection a judgement rather than a description?

items.text: It said what she did, why it worked, and what she would do again.
It gave a fuller account of what happened in the meeting.
It was longer than Tom's reflection.
It named the other team members and their roles.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara weighed her own actions and drew a lesson, which is more than description.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the reflection concluded about Amara's own performance, not how much it described.
feedback.incorrectFinal: It was a judgement because it weighed what Amara did, why it worked, and what she would repeat. A fuller or longer account of events is still description.
